Verily Health is a data platform and technology company purpose-built to power AI-enabled precision health solutions that accelerate research and improve care for individuals and communities. You will apply frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) and advanced machine learning techniques to extract deep clinical meaning from messy, unstructured medical text, turning fragmented healthcare data into trustworthy, analysis-ready longitudinal datasets. Job Description

BUSINESS TITLE: Basic Life Research Scientist

Work Schedule

Hybrid work arrangement

Budgeted Salary

The expected pay range for this position is $71,000 to $108,000 per annum.

School/Unit Description

The Stanford Digital Brain Project is a five-year, multi-investigator initiative to build a foundation model of the healthy adult human brain. We are collecting deep, stimulus-driven brain imaging data at unprecedented scale using 7T fMRI and OPM-MEG, with data organized into sequential scientific tranches and released publicly along with trained models and benchmarks. The project involves faculty across Stanford neuroscience, psychology, and computer science, purpose-built imaging facilities, and external compute partnerships. Data collection for the first tranche is beginning now.

Position Summary

We are hiring a scientific project manager to serve as the operational backbone of the project during its most intensive phase. The project runs through five working groups (7T fMRI, OPM-MEG, Tranche 1 design, informatics, computational modeling) led by faculty who are also running labs. Progress currently depends on faculty and a small staff absorbing coordination work that has outgrown them. You would take that on. This is a tactical, embedded role. You will sit inside the working groups, not above them. You will know what every group is doing this week, what is blocking them, and who owes what to whom. You will work alongside the project's executive leadership, who handle strategy, governance, and external partnerships, and you will be the person who makes sure decisions made on Friday still exist on Monday.

This is a two year, fixed term position.

What you will do

Track milestones, dependencies, and action items across all working groups; maintain the project's integrated plan and make status visible to the steering committee without anyone having to ask
Attend working group and steering committee meetings; capture decisions, owners, and open questions in a form the project can rely on
Chase and close the loop: unowned actions, stalled dependencies, and cross-group handoffs (for example, connecting an acquisition pipeline to a processing pipeline, or a stimulus freeze to a manifest build)
Coordinate operational logistics around data collection readiness: vendor timelines, equipment evaluation, facility scheduling, pilot experiment sequencing
Support hiring operations: candidate tracking, outreach coordination, onboarding of postdocs, research coordinators, and technical staff
Prepare pre-reads and decision memos so steering committee time goes to decisions rather than status
Maintain the project's tracking infrastructure (Google Workspace based; deliberately simple)

Required

PREFERRED/DESIRED QUALIFICATIONS:

PhD in neuroscience, cognitive science, psychology, or a related field, or equivalent research experience. You need enough domain fluency to follow a discussion about noise ceilings, retention functions, or preprocessing pipelines and know what matters and what is blocking
Experience with human neuroimaging research operations (fMRI, MEG/EEG, or similar); familiarity with what it takes to run participants at scale is a strong plus
Demonstrated ability to run coordination for a multi-stakeholder project: you have owned a tracker that people actually trusted
Comfort working with senior faculty as a peer in the room and holding them to owners and dates without friction
Bias toward lightweight tools and written records over process ceremony
Comfort with ambiguity; this project is being built while it runs

jobs.title: Linguist - Speech & Conversational AI
jobs.description:
Besimple AI is building datasets, benchmarks, and training environments that help voice models understand people, interact naturally, and complete real tasks.

We’re looking for a linguist to help define and improve the quality of the speech and conversations used to train these models. You’ll bring a trained ear for language, an understanding of how people communicate, and the ability to explain what makes a conversation clear, natural, and appropriate to its context.

Your work will connect linguistic expertise with practical decisions: which recordings are suitable for training, how contributors should be evaluated, what annotators should label, and how we measure the behavior of conversational agents.

What you’ll work on

Evaluate speech and conversational quality. Assess pronunciation, intelligibility, prosody, pacing, tone, and turn-taking in human recordings and model outputs. Explain why a response sounds natural, awkward, overly scripted, or inappropriate for the situation.
Build quality standards and evaluation rubrics. Translate customer requirements and feedback into clear criteria, examples, and decision rules. Define what reviewers should accept, flag, or reject, including how expectations differ across conversational roles and tasks.
Screen and support speech contributors. Help design auditions, evaluate recordings, and give actionable feedback on delivery. Identify contributors who can sustain natural conversations while following a scenario’s requirements.
Create and review linguistic annotations. Develop guidelines and reference examples for transcripts, speaker turns, speech delivery, and conversational behavior. Review human and model-generated labels, resolve ambiguous cases, and improve consistency across reviewers.
Improve conversational tasks and model evaluation. Work with researchers to refine scenarios, instructions, and turn-level rubrics. Identify unclear wording or grading criteria, and distinguish real model failures from problems in the task itself.
Turn recurring problems into better workflows. Analyze disagreements and rejection patterns, calibrate reviewers, and improve guidance in the crowdsourcing platform we build. Partner with engineers and audio specialists to separate language and delivery issues from recording defects.

What we’re looking for

A background in linguistics, speech science, phonetics, phonology, or a related field, through academic study or substantial applied experience.
Strong listening and analytical skills, with the ability to describe specific features of speech and explain how they affect meaning, clarity, and naturalness.
Experience with speech data, linguistic annotation, transcription, language assessment, or conversational analysis.
The ability to turn nuanced judgments into guidelines that other people can apply consistently.
Clear written communication and comfort giving specific, constructive feedback.
Careful judgment about ambiguity, language variation, and the difference between personal preference and a task’s actual requirements.

We welcome recent graduates with relevant research or substantial projects, as well as linguists with industry experience. Research, annotation guidelines, evaluation studies, and examples of applied linguistic work are all useful evidence.

Especially relevant experience

Evaluating text-to-speech, speech recognition, speech-to-speech, or conversational AI systems.
Prosody, pragmatics, discourse analysis, sociolinguistics, or conversation analysis.
Praat, ELAN, phonetic transcription, or other speech-analysis and annotation tools.
Designing annotation schemes, building reference datasets, or measuring agreement between reviewers.
Speaker auditions, voice coaching, or evaluating spoken performance.
Working with multilingual datasets or collaborating with linguists across languages.
Basic scripting or data analysis for investigating annotation quality and recurring errors.

You do not need experience in every area listed above.

Why this role

You’ll help shape the standards behind the data that voice models learn from. Your judgments will influence how we collect conversations, select speakers, evaluate model behavior, and improve the quality of our datasets.

This is an opportunity to apply linguistic expertise directly to the development of conversational AI, with ownership over both the quality of individual examples and the processes that make that quality repeatable.

jobs.description:
About Elicit

Elicit helps research and business teams investigate hard questions and make high-stakes decisions grounded in evidence.

Our ambition is to make high-quality reasoning under uncertainty available at a much greater scale in contexts where stakes are high and feedback is sparse. We're building AI systems whose work people can inspect, question, and improve, so that increasingly capable AI also makes us more wise.

Why we're hiring for this role

Some of the most valuable questions people face are also the hardest to answer well. Which research program should a team advance? What evidence would change its priorities? Which uncertainty is worth resolving before committing to a multi-year, $100 million dollar trial?

Today's models can contribute to these decisions, but they often miss a crucial consideration, make an assumption they should have checked, or reverse a recommendation too readily when presented with new information. Further, because they can perform increasing amounts of work autonomously, their process and reasoning is often poorly legible, so decision makers are wary to trust their outputs. Helping with these problems requires a deep understanding of model behaviors, what matters for different types of decisions, the environments and cultures in which decisions are made, and how to evaluate complex, multiplayer systems with many human and agent interactions.

We're looking for someone to own that work: understand where our systems fall short, develop ways to evaluate them, and build improvements that help users make better decisions. You'll start with concrete problems in scientific R&D and commercial strategy, and develop approaches that apply across different kinds of decisions.

About The Role

You'll join our engineering team and report to an Engineering Manager. You'll work on a cross-functional engineering team, collaborating closely with other engineers, product, design, and domain experts, taking problems from investigation and experimental design through implementation and use in the product.

The work combines careful reasoning, the ability to dive into domain specifics, and software design. You'll design agent environments and how agents represent problems, gather evidence, use tools, retain context, revise their conclusions, and coordinate with each other. You'll also make the engineering decisions that let us inspect those processes, test changes, and build on what works.

Most of the initial work will involve systems built around existing frontier models. Training or finetuning may be useful for particular problems, but the direction of the work will follow what helps users reason better.

What you'll own

Understand the decisions we're helping people make. Work through real cases with users and domain experts. Identify their objectives, constraints, available evidence, and important unknowns. Learn enough about an unfamiliar problem to recognize when an answer misses the point.
Define and measure good reasoning. Build evaluations for problems where success is initially underspecified. Combine close inspection of examples, expert judgment, and quantitative analysis. Investigate whether a better score reflects a meaningful improvement, and whether that improvement holds on new cases.
Improve the system's behavior. Turn observed failures into hypotheses you can test. Experiment with problem decomposition, context, tools, and ways for agents to seek information or check their work. Follow promising results through to changes users can benefit from.
Design the software that makes this work reliable. Choose useful abstractions, data structures, and component boundaries for reasoning workflows and evaluations. Make deliberate tradeoffs among simplicity, flexibility, reliability, latency, and cost. Build systems whose failures you and your teammates can diagnose.
Own the quality of what you ship. Write maintainable code, participate in design and code reviews, and test and monitor your changes. Work with other engineers to integrate your systems into the product and improve them as you learn from real use.

Example projects

Build and evaluate a workflow that helps a research team compare potential protein targets they could nominate for drug development, works in light of their goals and decision frameworks, performs legible research against detailed and stress-tested theories of success, and stays up to date in light of new findings.
Investigate why an agent overreacts to newly introduced evidence when forecasting clinical trial readouts. Create an evaluation that distinguishes justified changes in judgment from inconsistent ones, then implement and test an improvement.
Design a representation of evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions that an agent can update as a decision to acquire a new asset evolves, while preserving the information needed to inspect its work.
Improve an agent's ability to notice missing context and ask useful questions before making a recommendation.
Test whether an approach that improves R&D prioritization decisions transfers to business development strategy, and use the result to decide what belongs in a shared component.

What you bring to the role

Rigorous thinking about ambiguous problems. You can make a vague question precise, identify hidden assumptions, weigh conflicting evidence, and explain what would change your mind. You can make progress while remaining clear about what you don't know. This might come from a range of backgrounds such as original research in economics or developing quantitative trading approaches under adversarial conditions.
Curiosity across domains and clear communication. You enjoy getting to grips with unfamiliar subjects, learning from specialists, and explaining your reasoning to people with different expertise. A good sign is having leveraged domain expertise across multiple scientific domains or business specialities.
Good experimental instincts. You can devise a useful test when there isn't an established benchmark, distinguish evidence from noise, and recognize when your evaluation is rewarding the wrong behavior. You're willing to inspect individual failures in detail.
The ability to implement your ideas. You can independently write and debug code, work with data and model APIs, and take an experiment into a maintained codebase. You're comfortable with Python or a comparable language and willing to work across the relevant parts of our stack.
Practical familiarity with language models. You've explored their capabilities and limitations enough to have informed ideas about how to improve them. You can choose an approach based on the problem and update it as models change.
Strong engineering and architectural judgment. You can design a coherent system, explain your choices, and recognize when an abstraction helps or adds unnecessary complexity. You've built software that others can understand, use, and extend. Experience may come from products, research systems, or other substantial technical projects; a full-stack engineering background is not required.
Effective use of coding assistants. You use AI tools to increase what you can build while taking responsibility for understanding the design and verifying the result.

We care about evidence of these abilities. Substantial projects, thoughtful experiments, and clear explanations of technical decisions are useful ways to show us how you work.

Am I a good fit?

You might enjoy this role if you find yourself wanting to work through questions like these:

A model's recommendation sounds convincing to non-experts, but an expert thinks it is supported by slop. How would you investigate the disagreement and turn what you learn into a useful evaluation?
An agent has acquired new evidence. How should the agent identify which conclusions need revisiting, and how would you test that it does so correctly? How does this scale as the amount of evidence grows to tens of thousands of documents?
A workflow succeeds on a handful of simple examples. What would you need to learn before using it for customers, and which parts of the implementation would you change first?

You don't need a rehearsed answer. We'd like to understand how you approach problems like these, what you would build, and how you would learn whether it worked.

Location and travel

We have a great office in Oakland, CA, and we'd love to see you there if you're local. That said, we're just as happy for you to work remotely. We do get the whole team together for a quarterly retreat somewhere fun, because in-person time matters to us.

Benefits and perks

In addition to working on important problems as part of a productive and positive team, we also offer great benefits (with some variation based on location):

Flexible work environment - work from our office in Oakland or remotely as long as you can travel to work in-person for retreats and coworking events
Fully covered health, dental, vision, and life insurance for you, generous coverage for the rest of your family (FSA/HSA, too)
Flexible vacation policy, with a minimum recommendation of 20 days / year and plenty of company holidays
Every Elician receives a $200 monthly wellbeing stipend to spend on whatever supports your health and wellbeing.
401K with a 6% employer match
A new Mac + $1,000 budget to set up your workstation or home office in your first year, then $500 every year thereafter
$1,000 quarterly AI Experimentation & Learning budget, so you can freely experiment with new AI tools to incorporate into your workflow, take courses, purchase educational resources, or attend AI-focused conferences and events
A team administrative assistant who can help you with personal and work tasks
You can find more reasons to work with us in this thread!

Compensation

For all roles at Elicit, we use a data-backed compensation framework to make sure our salaries are market-competitive, equitable, and simple. For this role, we're targeting starting ranges of:

Career (L3): $185-220K + equity
Senior (L4): $220-260K + equity
Expert/Staff (L5): $250-320K + significant equity

We're optimizing for a hire who can contribute at a L4/senior-level or above. We'd love to meet staff/principal level contributors as well.

We also offer above-market equity for all roles at Elicit, as well as employee-friendly equity terms.

new_jobs.description:
About Elicit

Elicit helps research and business teams investigate hard questions and make high-stakes decisions grounded in evidence.

Our ambition is to make high-quality reasoning under uncertainty available at a much greater scale in contexts where stakes are high and feedback is sparse. We're building AI systems whose work people can inspect, question, and improve, so that increasingly capable AI also makes us more wise.

Why we're hiring for this role

Some of the most valuable questions people face are also the hardest to answer well. Which research program should a team advance? What evidence would change its priorities? Which uncertainty is worth resolving before committing to a multi-year, $100 million dollar trial?

Today's models can contribute to these decisions, but they often miss a crucial consideration, make an assumption they should have checked, or reverse a recommendation too readily when presented with new information. Further, because they can perform increasing amounts of work autonomously, their process and reasoning is often poorly legible, so decision makers are wary to trust their outputs. Helping with these problems requires a deep understanding of model behaviors, what matters for different types of decisions, the environments and cultures in which decisions are made, and how to evaluate complex, multiplayer systems with many human and agent interactions.

We're looking for someone to own that work: understand where our systems fall short, develop ways to evaluate them, and build improvements that help users make better decisions. You'll start with concrete problems in scientific R&D and commercial strategy, and develop approaches that apply across different kinds of decisions.

About The Role

You'll join our engineering team and report to an Engineering Manager. You'll work on a cross-functional engineering team, collaborating closely with other engineers, product, design, and domain experts, taking problems from investigation and experimental design through implementation and use in the product.

The work combines careful reasoning, the ability to dive into domain specifics, and software design. You'll design agent environments and how agents represent problems, gather evidence, use tools, retain context, revise their conclusions, and coordinate with each other. You'll also make the engineering decisions that let us inspect those processes, test changes, and build on what works.

Most of the initial work will involve systems built around existing frontier models. Training or finetuning may be useful for particular problems, but the direction of the work will follow what helps users reason better.

What you'll own

Understand the decisions we're helping people make. Work through real cases with users and domain experts. Identify their objectives, constraints, available evidence, and important unknowns. Learn enough about an unfamiliar problem to recognize when an answer misses the point.
Define and measure good reasoning. Build evaluations for problems where success is initially underspecified. Combine close inspection of examples, expert judgment, and quantitative analysis. Investigate whether a better score reflects a meaningful improvement, and whether that improvement holds on new cases.
Improve the system's behavior. Turn observed failures into hypotheses you can test. Experiment with problem decomposition, context, tools, and ways for agents to seek information or check their work. Follow promising results through to changes users can benefit from.
Design the software that makes this work reliable. Choose useful abstractions, data structures, and component boundaries for reasoning workflows and evaluations. Make deliberate tradeoffs among simplicity, flexibility, reliability, latency, and cost. Build systems whose failures you and your teammates can diagnose.
Own the quality of what you ship. Write maintainable code, participate in design and code reviews, and test and monitor your changes. Work with other engineers to integrate your systems into the product and improve them as you learn from real use.

Example projects

Build and evaluate a workflow that helps a research team compare potential protein targets they could nominate for drug development, works in light of their goals and decision frameworks, performs legible research against detailed and stress-tested theories of success, and stays up to date in light of new findings.
Investigate why an agent overreacts to newly introduced evidence when forecasting clinical trial readouts. Create an evaluation that distinguishes justified changes in judgment from inconsistent ones, then implement and test an improvement.
Design a representation of evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions that an agent can update as a decision to acquire a new asset evolves, while preserving the information needed to inspect its work.
Improve an agent's ability to notice missing context and ask useful questions before making a recommendation.
Test whether an approach that improves R&D prioritization decisions transfers to business development strategy, and use the result to decide what belongs in a shared component.

What you bring to the role

Rigorous thinking about ambiguous problems. You can make a vague question precise, identify hidden assumptions, weigh conflicting evidence, and explain what would change your mind. You can make progress while remaining clear about what you don't know. This might come from a range of backgrounds such as original research in economics or developing quantitative trading approaches under adversarial conditions.
Curiosity across domains and clear communication. You enjoy getting to grips with unfamiliar subjects, learning from specialists, and explaining your reasoning to people with different expertise. A good sign is having leveraged domain expertise across multiple scientific domains or business specialities.
Good experimental instincts. You can devise a useful test when there isn't an established benchmark, distinguish evidence from noise, and recognize when your evaluation is rewarding the wrong behavior. You're willing to inspect individual failures in detail.
The ability to implement your ideas. You can independently write and debug code, work with data and model APIs, and take an experiment into a maintained codebase. You're comfortable with Python or a comparable language and willing to work across the relevant parts of our stack.
Practical familiarity with language models. You've explored their capabilities and limitations enough to have informed ideas about how to improve them. You can choose an approach based on the problem and update it as models change.
Strong engineering and architectural judgment. You can design a coherent system, explain your choices, and recognize when an abstraction helps or adds unnecessary complexity. You've built software that others can understand, use, and extend. Experience may come from products, research systems, or other substantial technical projects; a full-stack engineering background is not required.
Effective use of coding assistants. You use AI tools to increase what you can build while taking responsibility for understanding the design and verifying the result.

We care about evidence of these abilities. Substantial projects, thoughtful experiments, and clear explanations of technical decisions are useful ways to show us how you work.

Am I a good fit?

You might enjoy this role if you find yourself wanting to work through questions like these:

A model's recommendation sounds convincing to non-experts, but an expert thinks it is supported by slop. How would you investigate the disagreement and turn what you learn into a useful evaluation?
An agent has acquired new evidence. How should the agent identify which conclusions need revisiting, and how would you test that it does so correctly? How does this scale as the amount of evidence grows to tens of thousands of documents?
A workflow succeeds on a handful of simple examples. What would you need to learn before using it for customers, and which parts of the implementation would you change first?

You don't need a rehearsed answer. We'd like to understand how you approach problems like these, what you would build, and how you would learn whether it worked.

Location and travel

We have a great office in Oakland, CA, and we'd love to see you there if you're local. That said, we're just as happy for you to work remotely. We do get the whole team together for a quarterly retreat somewhere fun, because in-person time matters to us.

Benefits and perks

Flexible work environment - work from our office in Oakland or remotely as long as you can travel to work in-person for retreats and coworking events

Who We Are

Nuro is a self-driving technology company on a mission to make autonomy accessible to all. Founded in 2016, Nuro is building the world’s most scalable driver, combining cutting-edge AI with automotive-grade hardware. Nuro licenses its core technology, the Nuro Driver™, to support a wide range of applications, from robotaxis and commercial fleets to personally owned vehicles. With technology proven over years of self-driving deployments, Nuro gives automakers and mobility platforms a clear path to AVs at commercial scale, empowering a safer, richer, and more connected future.

About The Team

Frontier models are fungible. Any team can rent the same intelligence we can, and the model we build on today will be replaced within a month. What is not fungible is the infrastructure that decides whether an autonomous system's output can be trusted — evaluation, verification, and the discipline to gate on evidence instead of impressions. Nuro has spent a decade building exactly that discipline for a robot that drives on public roads, and this team turns it inward: we build the platform that lets AI agents operate autonomously inside Nuro's own engineering organization, under the same standard of proof we apply to the vehicle.

Our mandate is to amplify the output of every engineer and researcher at Nuro by 100x. Not a better IDE, not a faster build — a change in what a single person can attempt. That number is a target, not a claim, and reaching it depends on one thing above all: autonomous work has to be trustworthy enough to run unattended. So our central ambition is to build the most rigorous closed-loop evaluation system for AI work anywhere. Leverage follows from trust, and trust follows from measurement.

We operate as a startup inside a company that has already shipped a hard thing. Small team, no established playbook, direct access to compute and to the systems we are automating. You will work directly with engineering leadership and the CEO, and the decisions you make will be yours to make rather than yours to implement.

About The Role

Most teams building agents make design decisions by intuition and anecdote. Someone tries a new memory scheme, it feels better, it ships. We think that is the central failure of the field right now, and we are building this team to work the other way: every decision about how our agent systems are constructed should be settled by evidence.

You would not be starting from zero. We already operate a substantial agent system in production, a fleet of agents with an extensive library of skills and plugins, integrated into the tools our engineers use daily, serving real users with real work. So every hypothesis you form can be tested against genuine production traffic from your first month. And the system is now complex enough that intuition has stopped being sufficient to improve it, which is precisely why this role exists.

Everything this team builds is centered on frontier-lab transformer models. We are not inventing architectures. We are extracting the maximum from the best models that exist, and adapting them ourselves in the narrow places where our data gives us an advantage nobody else has.

Your charter has two halves. Make the system perform against real-world data,
not public benchmarks or tasks we invented to look good, but our codebase, our infrastructure, and our engineers' actual requests, with all the ambiguity that implies. The gap between benchmark performance and real-task performance is where most agent systems quietly fail. And turn any task into a closed loop
: for any workflow an agent takes on, you should be able to say what success looks like, where the evaluation data comes from, how signal is collected, and how results feed the next iteration.

Own the evaluation pipeline end to end.
Three stages, and the value is in owning all three:

Eval data collection. Where ground truth comes from. Mining production traces for labeled outcomes, capturing human accept/reject/edit signal as it happens, building task sets that reflect the real distribution of work rather than the tasks that are easy to score, and knowing when a model-based judge is trustworthy and when it is laundering an assumption.
Eval loop construction. Turning a fuzzy objective into a measurement that runs on every change. Noise floors, statistical standards for acceptance, task suites that resist gaming, and experiments designed for production settings where clean randomization is not always available.
Automated hill climbing. The payoff. Once a task has a trustworthy loop, improvement can be searched rather than hand-crafted — prompts, context strategies, tool sets, routing, reasoning budgets, eventually model choice. This only works if the first two stages are sound; done wrong, it optimizes hard against a metric that means nothing. Post-train models on data nobody else has. This role includes hands-on model work: supervised fine-tuning and RL on open-source vision-language models, using the proprietary driving data Nuro has collected across years of real-world autonomous operation. You would have a labeling workforce available to you, which means you can specify the data you need rather than making do with what exists. Very few researchers get to run this loop, form a hypothesis about model behavior, commission the exact data to test it, post-train, and evaluate against real driving performance. The fungibility of frontier models is precisely why this matters: the weights are rentable, the data and the labeling capacity behind them are not.

Read the frontier and convert it into experiments.
The research frontier moves weekly, and most of it is noise. You are the person who reads it, separates results that will hold from those that will not replicate, and turns the ones that matter into live experiments against our workloads. This is a deliverable, not background reading — our architecture should reflect the best of what is publicly known within weeks of it becoming known.

Test-time scaling.
We believe the largest near-term gains come from how inference compute is spent, not from which model is called: reasoning budgets, sampling and search strategies, verifier-guided selection, when to escalate and when to stop. Each buys accuracy at a price, and the exchange rate differs by task. Mapping where additional inference compute pays and where a verifier beats a bigger model is a core agenda here, and it directly determines how we spend a real budget.

Across all of this, we want someone fluent at four levels: frontier models
and how they are built; frontier model evaluation
and where measurements lie; frontier AI system evaluation,
an agent is a model plus tools, memory, retries, verifiers, and a human who accepts or rejects the output, and the compound system fails in ways none of its parts do; and real-world impact, quantified
, with the integrity to say when the numbers do not support the story.

About The Work

You will work in close partnership with the engineer who builds the platform this runs on: they make it run safely at scale, you determine what it should be doing and whether it worked.

What You Might Own in Your First Two Quarters

Establish the evaluation foundation for the agent fleet we already run: eval data sources, task suites, noise floors, and the statistical standard the team uses to accept or reject a change.
Take one high-volume workflow from unmeasured to automatically hill-climbing, end to end, as the template the rest of the system follows.
Run a first post-training experiment on an open-weight VLM against our driving data, and establish whether the result justifies the pipeline.
Put a defensible number on what the platform is worth: which workflows improved, by how much, with what confidence.

About You

The person we are looking for probably has an engineering background and strong research taste, in that order of surprise. Researchers who can ship are common enough to name; researchers who can ship, judge a literature, and care more about scaled impact than authorship are not. If you have been frustrated by how long it takes good research to reach anything real, this role is the correction.

Graduate degree in CS, ML, statistics, or a related field, or equivalent research experience. We care about demonstrated research judgment, not credentials.
Fluent in the current literature and able to judge it. You read papers continuously, can tell a real result from a well-marketed one, and have opinions about which recent directions are overrated.
Deep understanding of how LLMs work — pretraining through the post-training stack, and what actually happens at inference. You reason from mechanism, not just from published numbers.
Firm grasp of the full evaluation pipeline: sourcing eval data, constructing the loop, automating the climb. Having done all three for a real system, rather than one in isolation, is the strongest signal for this role.
Rigorous experimentalist. You design experiments that can fail, you understand variance and power, and you are comfortable saying an intervention didn't work.
Hands-on post-training experience — SFT and RL, ideally on open-weight models — including the data curation and evaluation work required to know whether it actually helped. Vision-language model experience is a strong plus.
A real engineering background. Strong Python, comfortable with production systems and data, able to stand up the infrastructure your own experiment needs.
Direct experience with LLM agent systems — building them, evaluating them, or studying why they fail.
You measure yourself in impact and in weeks. You want your work in front of hundreds of engineers this quarter.

Bonus Points

Published or applied work in agent evaluation, reasoning, test-time compute, RL, or verification.
Experience with multimodal or vision-language models, and with data curation at scale.
Online experimentation in production: A/B testing, causal inference from observational data, offline-to-online correlation.
Experience building evaluation harnesses, task suites, or LLM-as-judge systems, including their failure modes.
Familiarity with autonomous systems, safety cases, or verification-gated deployment.

ML Engineer & Research Scientist, Speech (Full-time)
Location: San Francisco · Type: Full-time 

About Voice Arena
Voice Arena builds frontier evals, models and datasets for voice AI. Our mission is to make machines talk like humans, and to measure honestly how close they are.
We run public leaderboards for speech to text, text to speech, speech to speech and speaker diarization, with many more yet to come. Labs, voice platforms and enterprises use them to see how speech models perform on real speech, in real conditions and across languages, rather than on clean read audio.
Behind the boards is a research and engineering team that builds its own datasets, trains the models that keep its evaluations accurate and publishes its methods. What sets us apart:
Research that gets published.
Three papers at Interspeech 2026, where Voice Arena is also the Diamond Sponsor. Our methods go through peer review, not just a blog post.
Partners across the field.
We brought Hindi and Indian English to Hugging Face's Open ASR Leaderboard, and we partner with NVIDIA. Model providers send us new models for public and private evaluation.
Data nobody else has.
Monsoon, our dataset initiative for the Global South, is working towards 1,000 languages by 2027. Our accented English corpus covers 8 accents and 6,000 hours. This data gives us held-out test sets that models have not seen in training.
A research community.
Voice Research Club runs paper-first sessions for voice AI researchers, starting in San Francisco and New York, with more cities to follow.

About the role
Our mission is to make machines talk like humans. Before that is an engineering problem, it is a research problem: someone has to define what talking like a human actually means, measure how far today's models are from it, and show what closes the gap.
We're hiring an ML Engineer & Research Scientist to own that problem end to end. This role blends fundamental research and hands-on engineering, and we don't separate the two. You will decide which behaviours the best voice models should have, build the evals that measure them, define the data that teaches them, and train the models that prove it works on our leaderboards and others.
The core question for this role is simple: what does a speech model need to do to talk like a human, and how do we prove when it does?
This is a highly autonomous role. You'll work directly with the founders in a small, talent-dense team, with real ownership from day one. Everything you ship is public. When a new speech model launches, labs and enterprises check our boards to see where it stands, so your evals decide what gets measured and your models show the field what is possible.

In this role, you will
The work is one end-to-end research loop. You'll run it again and again, each time on a different open problem in speech:
Identify the problems in speech.
Find the gaps between today's speech models and machines that talk like humans, across recognition, synthesis, turn-taking, conversation, emotion, languages and accents. Listen to where models fail, read the literature, talk to the labs and users who hit these failures every day, and turn what you find into clear problem statements.
Define the behaviour we want models to have.
For each problem, write down precisely how a model should behave: what a good response sounds like, what counts as a failure, and where the line between them sits. This becomes the target labs build towards.
Design the evals.
Turn that behaviour into a measurement: test sets, automatic metrics, and human evaluation protocols where metrics fall short. Run current models through it and show where they stand and where they break.
Define the datasets.
Specify the data that would teach models the missing behaviour: what to record, from whom, in which languages and conditions, and how to label it. Our operations team builds it to your spec, and you own its quality.
Train models on that data.
Train and fine-tune models on the new data to prove it works. You'll be responsible both for making the numbers go up and for making sure the numbers mean something. The bar: models that climb our evals, our leaderboards and other public leaderboards.
Publish and open-source.
Write up the problem, the eval, the data and the results, and release the models. We want this work to be cited and built on, not just shipped.

In a typical week, you might:
Listen to hundreds of model outputs to find a failure that no metric is catching yet
Write the spec for a new eval and review the first batch of test data with the operations team
Run training runs and ablations, and dig into results that don't quite make sense
Check a new model launch against our boards and explain what its scores really mean
Talk to researchers at labs about the problems they are stuck on
Write up results for a paper, a blog post or a leaderboard release

What matters most
Everything in the loop serves two outcomes. They are how this role will be measured.
1. Building the right evals

An eval only matters if climbing it means real progress. Many speech benchmarks saturate, or reward models that learn the test instead of the skill. You'll own making sure a better score on our evals means a model is genuinely closer to the frontier of voice AI and to machines that talk like humans. You should be able to say what an eval measures, what it misses, and how it could be gamed. In practice:
Start from behaviour.
Every eval begins with a behaviour we want models to have, not with a metric that happens to be easy to compute.
Check against people.
Validate that scores agree with what human listeners actually prefer, and use human evaluation where automatic metrics fall short.
Keep it hard to game.
Use held-out and refreshed test sets, watch for contamination, and retire an eval once it stops separating good models from great ones.
Cover real speech.
Test across languages, accents, code-mixing, noise and real conversation, not only clean, read English.
Be rigorous.
Report confidence intervals, and tell real effects apart from noise and bugs before calling a ranking.

2. Building the models

Evals tell the field where to go; models prove the path works. You'll train models on the data you defined and show that they climb, so the behaviours we set and the data we design are backed by results, not opinion. In practice:
Train and fine-tune.
Work with open ASR, TTS and speech to speech models, fine-tuning them on the datasets built to your spec.
Prove what caused the gain.
Run clean ablations against honest baselines, so the improvement is shown to come from the new data and behaviour, not from tuning to the test.
Climb public boards.
Move up our leaderboards and other existing ones, such as Hugging Face's Open ASR Leaderboard, with results others can reproduce.
Train efficiently.
Keep training runs reproducible and make the most of every GPU hour.
Release openly.
Open-source the models with clear model cards, so labs and researchers can build on them.

What we offer
Hard, open problems.
Own the research questions that decide whether machines can talk like humans, across recognition, synthesis and conversation.
Open-source models.
Release the models you train, under your name.
Co-authorship on papers.
Co-author our papers at Interspeech, ICASSP and other top venues.
Real impact.
Your evals shape how labs build speech models and how the industry chooses between them.

Minimum qualifications
An MS or PhD in speech, ML or NLP, or an equivalent industry research
record
Strong Python and PyTorch,
and comfort with large audio datasets
Statistical care: you know when a ranking difference is real and when it is noise
Informed opinions about where voice AI is heading, not just familiarity with the tools
Solid engineering habits: version control, tests, reproducible experiments and pipelines others can run

Preferred qualifications
You don't need to match every bullet. Apply even if you meet only some of these.
Papers at Interspeech, ICASSP, ACL, NeurIPS
or similar
Experience with multilingual, low-resource or code-mixed speech
Work at a speech lab or voice AI company 
A benchmark, dataset or open-source tool others in the field use
Experience running GPU training or inference at scale
Experience designing human evaluation or annotation studies

Why join Voice Arena
Shape how voice AI gets built.
Labs, voice platforms and enterprises use our boards to decide which models to build, ship and buy.
See every model first.
Work with the newest speech models across languages, often before most of the field has tried them.
Publish and be seen.
Your work goes to Interspeech and ICASSP, to Hugging Face, and out to the voice AI community on X and LinkedIn.
Measure the whole world's speech.
Our data and evals reach far beyond English, across the wider Global South.
Join early.
Join a small, talent-dense team early, and shape the product, the team and the research agenda.

Send your CV, a short note and work you're proud of to amritansh@voicearena.com.
